normalized.governing_thought: Fix promotions, shrink and delivery, not wages: six moves reach a 3.2% margin by FY2028
executive_summary: Margin fell mainly through promotions, shrink and e-commerce, not wages
– Gross margin and e-commerce explain nearly four-fifths of the fall from 3.4% to 1.0%
– Hourly pay rose 9.4%, but fewer hours per sale absorbed about 70% of it
Promotions, shrink and private label can win back about $14M of gross margin a year
– 38% of promotions lost money; returning to the FY2024 share adds about $5.9M
– Fixing shrink in the least-staffed stores adds about $3.8M
E-commerce loses about $10M a year; repricing home delivery adds $2.8M
– Each home delivery loses about $12 after the fee; the fee test kept 98% of online sales
Targeted labor cuts and nine store exits save about $14M a year
– The proposed 8% cut risks about $7.5M of its $14.5M saving in extra shrink
– Six stores close at lease end; three repay their $7.5M exit in 3.4 years
Promotions, delivery fees and labor go first, reaching about 3.2% by FY2028
– Under a third of the first wave's $16M in FY2026 clears the $20M covenant
– Stretch levers worth $8.4M cover a 2027 wage rise of up to $7.3M

slides.title: Reversing the margin decline
Key questions

claims.claim: How can Harlow lift operating margin from 1.0% to at least 3.0% by FY2028, within $25M of one-time cost and the FY2026 covenant, and what comes first?
evidence: Decision maker: CEO, presenting the margin plan for board approval

Success criteria: Operating margin of at least 3.0% by FY2028; At most $25M of one-time cost or capital over FY2026–FY2028; Operating income of at least $20M in FY2026 (lender covenant); No closure of a store with a lease beyond 2027 without a board vote; delivery kept in some form
Timing: Board meeting, February 2027
Out of scope: Closing the e-commerce service; Broad price increases and new stores; Refinancing or covenant renegotiation

Sub-questions: 1 What drove operating margin from 3.4% to 1.0% between FY2023 and FY2025? 2 How much gross margin can promotions, shrink and private label win back? 3 Can Harlow keep home delivery and stop e-commerce losing money? 4 Where should store labor and the store network be cut, and where not? 5 Does the plan reach 3.0% by FY2028 within the constraints, and what comes first?

slides.title: Executive summary

claims.claim: Fix promotions, shrink and delivery, not wages: six moves reach a 3.2% margin by FY2028
evidence: Five numbered points with page references p. 5–7, 9–15, 17–23, 25–31, 33–38 (see executive_summary)

slides.title: Where the margin went
Gross margin and e-commerce fulfillment explain nearly four-fifths of the margin decline, store labor only an eighth

claims.claim: 79% of the margin decline comes from gross margin and e-commerce fulfillment
evidence: Chart: FY2023 margin 0.0337; Gross margin step 0.01019; Store labor 0.002996; Occupancy and energy 0.001985; E-commerce fulfillment 0.008381; FY2025 margin 0.0102

claims.claim: Gross margin: the largest step, driven by deeper promotions and higher shrink
E-commerce fulfillment: rose from 0.4% to 1.2% of sales as orders tripled and more went to the home
evidence: 0.4% to 1.2% of sales

claims.claim: Store labor: a small step despite a 9.4% rise in hourly pay, because hours per sale fell
evidence: 9.4% rise in hourly pay

claims.claim: Other SG&A held at 4.7% of sales and is left out; steps sum to the margin change within rounding
evidence: Other SG&A 4.7% of sales

slides.title: Wage inflation is real, but fewer labor hours per sale absorbed about 70% of it

claims.claim: 69.6% of the wage effect was offset by scheduling fewer hours per sale
evidence: Chart: FY2023 labor cost 0.117936; Higher hourly wage +0.011092; Fewer hours per sale −0.00772; FY2025 labor cost 0.121308

claims.claim: Hourly pay: up 9.4% in two years, as management says
Hours per sale: down 6% in the same two years, while shrink rose (1c)
Labor is the smallest big driver; more across-the-board hour cuts target the wrong cause
Rebuilt shares differ from the income statement (11.8% and 12.1%) by up to 0.03 percentage points through rounding

slides.title: Deeper promotions and higher shrink caused the fall in gross margin; private label offset only 15% of it

claims.claim: 15% of the promotion and shrink losses was won back by private-label growth
evidence: Chart: FY2023 gross margin 0.260423; More promotional sales −0.007; More private label +0.0018; Higher shrink −0.005; FY2025 gross margin 0.250233

claims.claim: Promotions: rose from 24% to 29% of sales, each sale earning 14 percentage points less margin
evidence: 24% to 29% of sales
14 percentage points less margin

claims.claim: Shrink: up from 2.1% to 2.6% of sales; fresh and produce waste is 45% of it
Private label: grew from 17% to 18.5% of sales at 12 percentage points more margin, too slowly to offset
evidence: 12 percentage points

slides.title: Where the margin went
Gross margin can win back about $14M a year from fewer money-losing promotions, less shrink and more private label

claims.claim: Promotions grew past paying back; the FY2024 share adds about $5.9M a year
evidence: 1a: 38% of FY2025 promotional events lost money

claims.claim: Deeper promotions have not held off ValuMart; shoppers come for fresh and convenience
evidence: 1b: −4.2% comparable sales near a new ValuMart

claims.claim: Shrink is highest where hours are thinnest; fixing the weakest half adds about $3.8M
evidence: 1c: 3.1% shrink in the least-staffed stores

claims.claim: Private label keeps its margin edge; holding its pace adds about $4.3M by FY2028
evidence: 1d: 12 pp more margin than national brands

claims.claim: Total $14M

slides.title: 1a: Promotions grew to 29% of sales while vendors funded a shrinking share of their markdowns

claims.claim: Promotional sales took a larger share every year
evidence: +5 pp
Promotional share: FY2023 24%; FY2024 26.2%; FY2025 29%

claims.claim: Vendors now fund less than half of the markdowns
evidence: −9 pp
Vendor-funded share: FY2023 55%; FY2025 46%

claims.claim: Each promotion now costs Harlow more of its own margin: vendor funding is the first negotiation
Markdown dollars are not in the briefing pack, so the funding lever is not sized and counts as upside

slides.title: 1a: Cutting promotions back to their FY2024 share of sales would recover about $5.9M of gross margin a year

claims.claim: Promotion reset recovers $5.9M gross margin a year
evidence: 2.8 pp of sales moved back to regular price: promotional share from 29.0% to the FY2024 level of 26.2%
× 14 pp more gross margin on each dollar sold at regular price (pack)
× $1,503M FY2025 sales
= $5.9M gross margin recovered a year

claims.claim: The cut comes from events that already lose money
evidence: The cut is about a tenth of promotional sales (9.7%), while 38% of FY2025 events lost money even after their extra units

claims.claim: Shoppers keep buying the items at regular price; the extra units the cut events sold are lost, which the review shows does not lower profit
Promotions stay in trade areas within three miles of a ValuMart; the cut is taken elsewhere
Vendor funding, down from 55% to 46% of markdowns, is not counted and is upside

slides.title: 1b: Deeper promotions have not held off ValuMart: nearby stores still lost sales and more shoppers call Harlow expensive

claims.claim: Stores near a new ValuMart still lost comparable sales
evidence: Comparable sales FY2025: within three miles of a new ValuMart −4.2%; other Harlow stores +1.1%

claims.claim: More shoppers now call Harlow expensive
evidence: +8 pp
More expensive: FY2023 33%; FY2025 41%

claims.claim: Price promotions are not winning against a discounter; shoppers name fresh produce and convenience as their reasons to choose Harlow
evidence: ValuMart has opened 11 stores in Harlow trade areas since 2023; category managers raised promotional depth in FY2024–FY2025
Customer survey, n = 3,100; top reasons: fresh produce 58%, convenience 44%

slides.title: 1c: Stores with the fewest labor hours per sale run about a third more shrink than the best-staffed stores

claims.claim: 1.3x the shrink rate of the best-staffed quartile, in the least-staffed quartile
evidence: Shrink FY2025: Q1 (fewest hours) 3.1%; Q2 2.7%; Q3 2.4%; Q4 (most hours) 2.3%
Chain average 2.6%

claims.claim: Q1: store managers say produce rotation and receiving checks are skipped on busy days
Q1 to Q3: the steepest part of the curve, where added hours cut shrink the most
Q3 to Q4: shrink barely moves, so extra hours there buy little
Move hours into rotation and receiving in Q1–Q2 stores and take cuts in Q3–Q4 stores (3a)
The pattern is a correlation across 58 stores; store managers' reports point to the mechanism
evidence: Waste and receiving errors are 65% of shrink, theft 35%

slides.title: 1c: Bringing shrink in the two least-staffed quartiles down to the Q3 rate would add about $3.8M a year

claims.claim: Shrink program recovers $3.8M gross margin a year
evidence: 1 pp combined excess of Q1 (3.1%) and Q2 (2.7%) over the Q3 rate of 2.4%
÷ 4 quartiles of equal sales: a 0.25 percentage point cut in chain shrink
× $1,503M FY2025 sales

claims.claim: Waste and receiving errors are the part that labor fixes
evidence: Fresh and produce waste (45%) and receiving and administrative errors (20%) make up 65% of shrink

claims.claim: Theft (35%) is not targeted by this program
The four quartiles carry equal sales; their simple average matches the 2.6% chain rate
Returning the whole chain to its FY2023 rate of 2.1% would double the gain; it is held as a stretch lever (5d)

slides.title: 1d: Holding private label's FY2025 growth pace would add about $4.3M of gross margin a year by FY2028

claims.claim: $4.3M gross margin added a year by FY2028
evidence: Private-label share: FY2023 17%; FY2024 17.7%; FY2025 18.5%; FY2028 at the same pace 20.9%
2.4 pp more share × 12 pp margin gap × $1,503M FY2025 sales

claims.claim: The gain comes from mix, not price
evidence: Margin edge: each private-label sale earns 12 percentage points more than a national brand

claims.claim: Pace held, not raised: only the FY2024–25 gain of 0.8 percentage points a year continues
Fits the price problem: a cheaper own brand answers the 41% who call Harlow expensive

slides.title: Where the margin went
E-commerce loses about $10M a year; repricing home delivery is the first fix and keeps the service the owners want

claims.claim: Counted in full, e-commerce loses money: the team's 6.1% leaves out the courier and counts every sale as new
evidence: 2a: −$10.4M e-commerce result, FY2025, all costs and only new sales counted

claims.claim: Home delivery causes the loss; a click-and-collect order loses under $2
evidence: 2b: −$12.3 result per delivered order after the fee, FY2025

claims.claim: Customers accept a higher fee by switching to pickup; a rollout adds about $2.8M a year
evidence: 2c: 98% of e-commerce sales kept in the fee test

slides.title: 2a: Counted in full, e-commerce loses about 8% of its sales rather than earning the 6.1% its team reports

claims.claim: Two corrections turn the reported profit into a $10.4M loss
evidence: E-commerce contribution: team's figure 6.1%; counted in full −8.1677%

claims.claim: Courier left out, −6.5 percentage points: finance books third-party delivery, net of fees, in its own line, so the team's figure never carries it
Every sale counted as new, −7.8 percentage points: customers say 70% of what they buy online they would otherwise buy in a Harlow store
Scale: at 8.5% of chain sales, this loss now moves the chain margin
evidence: 8.5% of chain sales

claims.claim: The 'every sale counted as new' correction is the remainder and also absorbs differences in packaging and cost allocation between the two methods
evidence: Full count: 20 cents of contribution per new dollar on the 30% of online sales new to Harlow, less all e-commerce fulfillment

slides.title: 2a: With only 30% of online sales new to Harlow, their contribution covers less than half the cost of fulfilling them

claims.claim: Contribution from new online sales covers 42.3% of fulfillment cost
evidence: $127.8M e-commerce sales, FY2025 (8.5% of chain sales)
× 30% new to Harlow (survey, n = 2,300)
× 20% contribution per new dollar before fulfillment (finance)
= $7.7M contribution from new online sales
÷ $18.1M fulfillment cost: picking plus courier, net of fees

claims.claim: The survey share holds for all online sales: 70% would otherwise have been bought in a Harlow store
Cannibalized sales earn the same margin online as in store, so they add nothing
Finance's 20 cents per new dollar is gross margin less variable store costs, before fulfillment

slides.title: 2b: Home delivery drives the loss: each delivered order loses about $12 once the courier is paid

claims.claim: 91.3% of the e-commerce loss comes from home delivery, 58% of orders
evidence: Per delivered order: Picking $7.40; Third-party delivery $13.80; Delivery fee collected −$3.10; Contribution from new sales −$5.76; Loss per delivered order $12.34

claims.claim: Courier: the largest cost in the order, and it rose every year while the fee fell
Fee: free delivery above $75 means the average delivered order pays only $3.10
Click-and-collect: carries picking but no courier, and loses under $2 an order
Contribution per order = $96 basket × 30% new to Harlow × 20 cents. Delivered and click-and-collect baskets assumed equal (the pack gives one average)
evidence: $96 basket

slides.title: 2c: The fee test kept 98% of online sales and more than doubled the fee collected per delivery

claims.claim: Fee test kept 98% of e-commerce sales
evidence: 4 stores, 10 weeks, late FY2025
Total online sales fell 2%
Delivered orders fell 9%
Most delivery customers switched to pickup rather than leaving
Delivery stays available, as the owners require

claims.claim: Average fee per delivered order $6.4
evidence: 2.1 times the FY2025 average of $3.10
Fee below the threshold raised from $4.99 to $7.99
Free-delivery threshold raised from $75 to $100
Still below the $13.80 courier cost

claims.claim: 14% more click-and-collect orders
evidence: Free for customers, no courier for Harlow
Each switch saves the courier cost of the order
Pickup costs only picking

claims.claim: Customers pay more for delivery, and those who will not switch to free pickup rather than leave

slides.title: 2c: Rolling out the tested fee and threshold chain-wide would add about $2.8M a year while keeping delivery

claims.claim: Repricing delivery adds $2.8M operating income a year
evidence: $18.1M e-commerce fulfillment cost, FY2025
− $15.1M fulfillment at the tested fee: 9% fewer deliveries, 14% more pickups, $6.40 a delivery
− $0.2M contribution lost on the 2% of online sales that leave

claims.claim: The test results hold chain-wide
evidence: Delivered orders fall 9% and click-and-collect orders rise 14% chain-wide, as in the 4-store, 10-week test
The average fee per delivered order reaches the test's $6.40; picking and courier costs per order stay at FY2025 levels
Sales lost (2%) are new to Harlow in the same 30% share as all online sales

claims.claim: The courier's proposed 3% rise is excluded; it is handled at the 2026 renewal (2c)

slides.title: 2c: Even at the tested fee each home delivery still loses about $9: the 2026 courier renewal is the next lever

claims.claim: Renegotiate the courier contract in 2026
evidence: The contract renews in 2026, and the provider has proposed a 3% rise
At $13.80 the courier is the largest cost in each delivered order
Tender against other couriers before accepting any increase
Owner: head of e-commerce
$0.3M a year avoided by rejecting the proposed 3% rise

claims.claim: Test a second fee step
evidence: The first test kept 98% of online sales at a $6.40 average fee
A second test in a few stores shows where demand starts to fall
Test in FY2026, decide in FY2027
$15.4 fee per delivered order at which delivery breaks even

claims.claim: Steer orders to click-and-collect
evidence: Pickup orders lose under $2 each and rose 14% in the test
Promote pickup at checkout and in the app
Add pickup capacity before delivery capacity
Supports the fee change

claims.claim: Each home delivery still loses about $9 at the tested fee
evidence: −$9.04 per delivered order at the tested fee
Break-even fee = picking ($7.40) + courier ($13.80) − contribution from new sales ($5.76) per delivered order, FY2025 costs

slides.title: Where the margin went
Store costs can fall by about $14M a year through targeted labor cuts and exits from loss-making stores

claims.claim: A net 4% cut taken in the best-staffed stores saves about $7.3M a year; the 8% cut risks half its saving in shrink
evidence: 3a: 51.8% of the 8% cut's saving lost if the chain ran at the Q1 shrink rate

claims.claim: Nine stores lose money; closing them adds about $6.6M a year, and six can close at lease end
evidence: 3b: 9 stores with negative four-wall EBITDA, FY2025

claims.claim: Total $13.9M

slides.title: 3a: Harlow has already cut hours per sale by 6%, and shrink rose half a percentage point over the same years

claims.claim: Stores already work fewer hours per sale
evidence: Labor hours per thousand dollars of sales: FY2023 7.02; FY2025 6.6

claims.claim: Shrink rose in the same two years
Another across-the-board cut would deepen a pattern already raising shrink (1c)

slides.title: 3a: The proposed 8% hours cut could give back about half of its $14.5M saving through higher shrink

claims.claim: 51.8% of the claimed saving lost to shrink in this scenario
evidence: Saving claimed for the 8% cut $14.5M; Shrink at the Q1 rate −$7.515M; Net saving $6.985M
0.5 pp Q1 shrink rate above the chain average (3.1% against 2.6%) × $1,503M FY2025 sales = −$7.5M

claims.claim: Shrink risk: Q1 stores already run 3.1% shrink against a 2.6% chain average, and the cut pushes every store toward Q1
Customer risk: checkout waits and stock-outs hit the fresh produce that 58% of shoppers come for
Not counted: sales lost to waits or empty shelves would cut the net further

slides.title: 3a: A net 4% cut in the best-staffed stores saves about $7.3M a year, close to what the 8% cut would net

claims.claim: Net 4%, targeted (recommended) saves $7.3M against $14.5M for the 8% across the board (management draft); once shrink is counted the 8% cut nets about $7.0M
evidence: Where hours are cut: every store vs Q3–Q4 stores; some hours moved to Q1–Q2
Shrink risk: up to $7.5M a year vs Low: Q3 and Q4 shrink differ by 0.1 percentage points
Fresh and receiving: cut with everything else vs protected, and added in Q1–Q2 stores
Customer risk: longer checkout waits and stock-outs chain-wide vs limited to the best-staffed stores
$181.9M store labor cost, FY2025 × 4% net cut (team choice) = $7.3M

slides.title: 3b: Nine of Harlow's stores lose money at the four-wall level, and six of their leases end by 2027

claims.claim: 9 of 58 stores have negative four-wall EBITDA, FY2025
evidence: Combined sales of $118M, 7.9% of the chain
Each one is below zero on its own result

claims.claim: −$3.1M combined four-wall EBITDA

Staff, rent and energy leave with the store

claims.claim: 6 of the nine leases end by 2027; no board vote needed

claims.claim: Six exits need only a decision not to renew; the other three are a board choice with a cost

slides.title: 3b: Closing all nine stores would add about $6.6M a year: $3.1M of losses removed and $3.5M from sales that move

evidence: $29.5M of the nine stores' $118M sales move to nearby Harlow stores (25%, past closures)

slides.title: 3b: Six stores can close at lease end at no cost; the other three repay their $7.5M exit in about 3.4 years

claims.claim: Three long-lease stores: $7.5M one-time cost, $2.2M a year, 3.4-year payback; worth the vote
evidence: $7.5M = 30% of the $25M cap

slides.title: Where the margin went
Six moves lift operating income to about $44.8M by FY2028, a 3.2% margin that clears the board's target

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: Approve the first wave now: it clears the covenant and carries over half of the gain. Six moves (promotion reset, targeted labor, delivery repricing, shrink program, private label, store exits) lift operating income to about $44.8M by FY2028, a 3.2% margin; promotions, delivery fees and targeted labor come first (about $16M a year, no store closures), replacing the 8% hours cut with the net 4% targeted plan, with six stores closed at lease end and the three long-lease exits brought to a board vote.

alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected in favour of a net 4% targeted cut in Q3–Q4 stores: the 8% cut's $14.5M saving could lose about $7.5M (51.8%) to higher shrink, netting about $7.0M, close to the targeted cut's $7.3M with far more risk.

alternatives_considered.option: Net 4% targeted labor cut in Q3–Q4 stores
alternatives_considered.treatment: Recommended; saves about $7.3M a year with low shrink risk.

alternatives_considered.option: Close only the six lease-end stores vs. all nine
alternatives_considered.treatment: Base case closes all nine; the three long-lease stores cost $7.5M and pay back in 3.4 years ('Worth the vote'); without them FY2028 margin lands at about 3.0% (2.98%), just under target.
Left out: 41% of shoppers already call Harlow expensive while ValuMart expands.

alternatives_considered.option: Holding wage rates below the market
alternatives_considered.treatment: Left out: set by the state minimum wage and a tight labor market.
Left out: the owners want delivery kept in some form.
Left out: flat at 4.7% of sales, no part of the decline.
Left out: leases are fixed until expiry; handled through store exits (3b).

alternatives_considered.option: Deeper promotions to defend against ValuMart (category team's case)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: counts the extra sales but not the margin; 38% of events lost money and stores near ValuMart still lost comparable sales.

alternatives_considered.option: Further delivery levers: renegotiate courier contract, second fee test, steer orders to click-and-collect
alternatives_considered.treatment: Presented as next levers since each delivery still loses about $9 at the tested fee; tender courier before accepting the proposed 3% rise; second test in FY2026, decide FY2027.

alternatives_considered.option: Stretch levers: promotions to the FY2023 share and chain shrink back to 2.1%
alternatives_considered.treatment: Held in reserve, worth $8.4M, to cover the 2027 minimum-wage rise of up to $7.3M.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Built only from the briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data)
No sales growth assumed to FY2028; moves sized on FY2025 sales/volumes
Plan figures are before the 2027 minimum-wage rise and stretch levers; the wage rise in full would cut FY2028 to $37.9M, 2.7%
Vendor funding lever not sized (markdown dollars not in pack); counted as upside
Promotion reset assumes shoppers buy cut items at regular price
Shrink–labor link is a correlation across 58 stores; store managers' reports point to the mechanism; assumes rotation and checks cut waste and errors
Theft (35% of shrink) is not targeted by the shrink program
Private label assumes the range can keep growing at 0.8 pp a year for three years
Delivery repricing assumes the 4-store, 10-week test represents the chain; picking and courier costs per order stay at FY2025 levels; lost sales new to Harlow in the same 30% share
Courier's proposed 3% rise (about $0.3M) excluded; handled at the 2026 renewal
Delivered and click-and-collect baskets assumed equal ($96; pack gives one average)
Survey share (70% would otherwise buy in store) assumed to hold for all online sales; cannibalized sales earn the same margin online as in store
Targeted labor assumes Q3–Q4 cuts leave shrink unchanged; 4% net cut is a team choice
Store exits assume past closures predict a 25% sales transfer at 12% contribution; average-size stores assumed; head-office cost and depreciation not counted; no turnaround plan in the pack
8% cut shrink scenario does not count sales lost to waits or empty shelves
Covenant test holds only if promotional share and shrink rise no further than FY2025 levels; each extra point of promotional share costs about $2.1M
FY2026 treated as first plan year and covenant year; if it is already largely past, the test rests on actions taken so far
Eight planning choices made without management input (CEO unavailable to confirm) and should be confirmed before the board meeting
Risks: 2027 minimum-wage rise (largest risk), traffic loss from fewer promotions, delivery customers leaving, closed-store sales not transferring
Rebuilt labor shares differ from income statement by up to 0.03 pp through rounding
